transcript.content: Hello, I’m Dr. [Name]. What brings you in today?

I'm here because I've been struggling with severe mood swings for about a year and two months now. I alternate between times when I feel extremely high-energy and irritable, and other times when I feel deeply depressed and lose interest in everything. It's just getting really hard to handle.
During your high or low mood episodes, have you ever had hallucinations or strong beliefs that others said were not true, even when your mood was not changed?

No, I've never experienced hallucinations or had those kinds of strong beliefs, especially not when my mood was normal. Any struggles I have seem to only happen when I'm in the middle of those high or low phases.

Have you ever had a high-energy or irritable episode that lasted at least a week and caused major problems, like needing hospitalization, acting very recklessly, or being unable to function at work or school?

Yes, absolutely. Those high-energy and irritable periods have lasted for a very long time, around a year and two months now. During these times, my energy is overflowing, my thoughts race constantly, and I get so easily irritated that it has severely disrupted my daily life and ability to function.

latest_inference.note: Previously the candidates were [Bipolar I Disorder, Bipolar II Disorder], but Bipolar II Disorder is now unlikely because the patient describes prolonged, severe high-energy/irritable episodes with major functional impairment, which is more consistent with full manic episodes than hypomanic episodes. There is also no history of psychosis outside mood episodes, so Bipolar I Disorder remains the best fit from the previous candidates.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient reports a prolonged history of clearly elevated/irritable mood with markedly increased energy, racing thoughts, and major functional impairment consistent with a manic episode, along with depressive episodes. He denies hallucinations or delusions outside mood episodes, making a primary psychotic disorder or schizoaffective disorder less likely. The severity and duration of the high-energy episodes support Bipolar I Disorder over Bipolar II Disorder.
